April 1, 1874] LIABILITY OE NATIVES OE INDIA TO ENTERIC EEVER, &c. 85 
ORIGINAL COMMUNICATIONS. 
OBSERVATIONS ON THE LIABILITY OF NATIVES OP 
INDIA TO ENTERIC FEVER, WITH NOTES OF CASES 
REPORTED from: ABBOTIABAD DURING THE LAST 
TWO YEARS. 
By Surgeon-Major J. K. Johnson, 5th GoorJcha Regiment^ and 
Civil Surgeon, Huzara District. 
In the Iiopa that details concerning even a few cases of 
undoubted enteric fever in natives of this country may not 
prove altogether uninteresting, I venture, in the accompanying 
appendix, to bring to the notice of my professional brethren 
some notes of cases of this disease which have occurred in my 
own practice at Abbottabad within the last two years. Enteric 
fever has been so ably delineated in most standard works on 
the Practice of Medicine, and is generally so easily recognized 
by experienced physicians, that particulars regarding its symptoms, progress, or post-mortem appearances would possess but 
little interest for the professional reader; were it not that the 
existence of the disease in natives of India is annually denied 
in the valuable reports published on the deservedly high 
authorities of the Sanitary Commissioner with the Government 
of India. So far as I can understand, this denial is based upon 
negative assumptions. No doubt, every assertion of the 
nature of that I am now combating must, in the necessity of 
the case, be based to a certain extent on negative inferences; 
but this consideration makes it all the more necessary that 
the appended cases should receive due publicity. I am unwilling to express decided opinions on the etiology of these 
cases. But I think I shall be supported by the experience of 
many fellow workers in native hospitals and civil dispensaries, when I state that we have hitherto done little towards 
any exact investigation of the fevers to which natives of 
India are subject; and, after much consideration of all the 
circumstances attending these cases, I am wholly unable to 
reconcile them with the theory of the exemption of natives

from enteric fever which has been advanced in the reports 
above quoted. I leave the cases to speak for themselves, aud 
proceed to offer some general observations on the subject. 
On looking over the dispensary and other local records, 
I have been unable to discover any thing of importance bearing on the history or prevalence of enteric fever in the district 
of Huzara. Many of my predecessors must have seen and 
recognized the disease and may hare published their experience. Should this be the case, I hope they will inform me 
where the records are to be found; while with, my present 
regiment for some months in 1865, I saw two cases of typhoid 
in Goorkhas. The accidental symptom of haemorrhage from 
the bowels drew my attention to these cases, and first suggested 
to my mind that natives were liable to suffer from this disease. 
The first cases in the civil dispensary returns appear in 
the records for 1867, and are thus commented on by. Dr. 
Farrell, who was then civil surgeon:?"Towards the end of 
the cold weather and early part of the spring (1867) a low 
typhoid fever extensively prevailed with the marked characteristics which this type of fever has shown in the Punjab. 
Of those cases treated as in-door patients, but few proved 
fatal, and I have not been able to ascertain the mortality in 
the cases where medicines were sent to the patients' homes. 
The peculiarities of this fever have been fully described." 
The next extract is from a report by Dr. Thorn, dated 1st 
January 1869. " On assuming charge I found the Native Dr. 
Wahid Ali labouring under typhoid fever. After a lingering 
illness the native doctor died. From 1867 up to the present 
time, a certain number of typhoid fever cases have annually 
appeared in the returns as treated in the Abbottabad dispeneury. Some intelligent natives of the district saw one or more 
of the eases numbered from 1 to 11 in the dispensary series, 
and assured me that the fever from which they were suffering 
was 
" Tup-i-Sutur," literally seven day fever, a common

affection in the district and known far and wide as a frequent 
cause of mortality in village communities- Natives describe 
it as often occurring in dropping cases, and now and again 
assuming an epidemic form. Spring is usually considered the 
time of its maximum prevalence. 
The local name Tup-i-Sutur is most likely a generic one for 
many forms of continued fever; but the symptoms described 
by villagers, such as constant diarrhoea and haemorrhage from 
the bowels, strongly favor the assumption that this fever is 
in many instances what we know as typhoid, and thereby 
corroborate the deductions which a mind unoccupied by any 
previously accepted theory would naturally draw from the not 
unfrequent occurrence of such cases in our dispensaries and 
regimental hospitals. It is my intention to take an early 
opportunity of further investigating the subject, and the civil 
authorities have promised to give me notice of the nest epidemic of malignant fever, which may be reported from the 
interior of the district. 
When noticing the prevalence of enteric fever in young 
British soldiers serving in India, Dr. Cuningham, in page 41 
of his interesting report for 1871, writes as follows : 
" There is good reason to conclude that the returns do not 
indicate all the cases which really occurred, and that not 
a few of the deaths ascribed to remittent and continued 
fevers were really caused by enteric fever." 
Dr. Brjden's numerous short extracts, concerning individual 
cases in the British army during the years 1871-72, show that 
in a country, where malarial fevers are the prevalent type, 
typhoid often escapes early detection ; and, in some of the 
recorded cases, its presence was not ascertained until after death. 
It may, therefore, be fairly assumed that if post-mortem investigations were the exception instead of being the rule in the 
British army, many more of the deaths caused by typhiod 
would be ascribed to other forms of fever. In the face of 
these facts it appears inconsistent to accept without reserve 
the results shown by the annual statements of fever mortality

in the Native army. If it is difficult to diagnose cases of 
typhoid in the European, and if it is a fact that even in deaths 
from fever among Europeans occurring in well-attended 
English hospitals in this country, the presence of typhoid 
is occasionally discovered only by post-mortem examination? 
hypothesis both of which are clearly established by Dr. 
Bryden's reports?I feel sure that no medical officer, who knows 
by practical experience the difficulties attending correct diagnosis of the diseases of native patients, and the disadvantages 
against which officers in charge of native hospitals have to contend, as compared with their confreres in European regiments, 
will accept the fever returns of the native army as adequate 
demonstration of the exemption of natives from enteric fever. 
We should bear in mind that, whereas it is the general 
practice to hold post-mortem examinations in European 
hospitals, it is the exception to do so in native ones. The 
Secretary to the Surgeon-Greneral, I. 'II. D., Calcutta, kindly furnished me on application, with returns showing how many 
of the fatal cases of fever in' the Native army in 1871 were 
made the subject of post-mortem examinations. The return 
proves that in only 5*30 per cent, of these cases were such 
examinations held. 
It will be admitted that statistics are valuable only so far 
as we can have confidence in their accuracy ; and where, as 
in the subject under review, post-mortem examinations are so 
necessary to accuracy and have been so rarely resorted to, but 
where from among the few deaths to which this test has been 
applied, we find cases, such as those .noted in the appendix, 
the whole course of which between admission aud death agrees 
g0 THE INDIAN MEDICAL GAZETTE. [April 1, 1874'. 
so remarkably with .what Dr. Brjden reports to be common 
experiences attending typhoid eases in European hospitals, 
an argument arises against the soundness of our preconceived 
ideas, concerning the exemption of natives from enteric fever,

which is to my mind of such a nature as to destroy all confidence in them, pending the result of wider and more accurate 
observation. There remains one other side to the argument 
which seems to me of much importance. The mortuary statistics of the Native army give us only a very incomplete view 
of the conditions of native life, for, obviously, they deal almost 
entirely with adults. To take an example, the force of which 
will be at once admitted by all, we find, on referring to the 
returns for 1871 (see extract in margin), that the Native 
Strength of Native 
Army in 1871 ... 54087'6 
Mortality from smallpox in 1871 ... 2 
army enjoys a very marked immunity from small-pox. Are we 
therefore to assume from this fact 
that our native soldiers are completely protected by vaccination ; or, knowing as we do that 
this is not the case, shall we account for what is evidently a 
point of high importance to the sanitary condition of the 
Native army by assuming such a comparative immunity of the 
population at large from this disease as we have so contentedly 
assumed in respect of typhoid fever from the non-appearance 
of such cases in the same statistics ? We well know that 
either assumption in respect of small-pox would be quite wrong, 
and that the true explanation of the immunity of the native 
army from epidemics of small-pox is to be found in the age 
at which our native soldiers are enlisted. The conditions of 
native life in the plains of India are notoriously such that, 
excepting the few cases in which natives are protected by vaccination, it is almost impossible for any of them to arrive at 
adult age without suffering from small pox. Now, we know 
that there are many points of analogy between small-pox and 
enteric fever, their principal difference being that the main 
characteristic of one is a copious cutaneous eruption, while that 
of the other consists in infiltration and ulceration of intestinal 
glands. The difference is unfortunately such as to enhance our 
difficulties in ascertaining the exteut to which enteric fever

prevails amongst the native population. If a village is suffering 
from an epidemic of small-pox, even the rudest native cannot 
have the smallest difficulty in recognizing it, but if the epidemic is one of enteric fever it is hardly to bo expected that, 
with our present limited machinery for sanitary inspection, we 
should know any thing about it. 
I think this argument, from the statistics of small-pox in the 
native army, is conclusive against the value of the same statistics as an adequate illustration of any supposed immunity of 
our native population from enteric fever. Before closing this 
paper I think it may be useful to notice a remark made by 
Dr. Brjden in a foot-note to the cases of typhoid fever reported 
in the native army in 1872 (vide margin). This may either 
In connection with this 
typhoid in Goorkhas, and 
the infiltration of the glands 
of Peyer and the mesenteric 
elands, it is interesting to 
note that four deaths in the 
native army from tuberculosis mesenterica occurred 
in Goorkhas. 
Vide Section III, page 
XXVII, Sanitary Commissioner's Keport for 1872. 
mean that a tubercular diathesis 
predisposes to enteric fever, or it 
may be intended to throw a doubt 
on the accuracy of the diagnosis 
in the cases reported as typhoid. 
Now, it has been asserted on good 
authority tliat the bowel lesions in 
enteric fever, or the malnutrition 
or debility consequent on severe 
attacks of that disease, often light up tubercular mischief which 
was previously dormant, but I cannot find it stated on any 
authority that the converse is known to occur, nor is it in the 
nature of tlie tubercular diathesis to tend to such a result. The 
very wide difference between the progress and pathological 
phenomena presented by these diseases is well illustrated by the 
appended abstract of my notes 011 a case of acute tuberculosis 
which occurred iu the 5:h Gooi kha Regiment last rear. I would

invite any one who i3 inclined to account for the typhoid cases 
reported in .the appendix upon the hypothesis indicated by 
Dr. Bryden to compare the notes of the acute tuberculosis 
case with those of Nos. 1, 2 and 4 of my regimental typhoid 
series. 
I hope to return the subject of these notes at a later date 
?when I shall have had further opportunities of making observations similar to those herewith reported. 
Abbottabad, 20th February 1874. 
Appendix containing notes of cases of Enteric Fever treated at 
Abbottabad within the last two years. 
The subject of the first case was a lad who marched into 
Abbottabad in a detachment of recently enlisted recruits on 
the 5th of June 1S72. In accordance with the prevailing custom of Goorkha Regiments, this draft, numbering upwards of 
100 lads, was enlisted at Goruckpore, on the confines of Nepal, 
and marched up-country to join head-quarters in the spring 
of 1872. 
Small-pox broke out amongst the recruits on the road and 
proved fatal in two instances. The native officer in command 
wisely checked the spread of this disease by keeping men 
previously unprotected by vaccination or inoculation one day's 
march in front of the protected men with whom the small-pox 
convalescents travelled. In this way, several unprotected men 
escaped small-pox, and, on reaching head-quarters, underwent 
successful vaccination. The fact of an infectious disease having 
appeared in the draft while en route to join the regiment 
secured for the men composing it, on their arrival in cantonments, an unusual degree of anxious solicitude. They were kept 
for some time in a separate quarantine camp, and daily subjected 
to searching examinations.* A medical inspection, with a view 
of separating the sick from the healthy, was carried out at once. 
Under the circumstances already stated, it was then necessary 
to ascertain what men were protected from small-pox, and to 
vaccinate those who were not protected ; so that the recruits 
underwent at least two close medical examinations on the 6th

and 7th of June, Dr. Banister, Deputy Surgeon-General, being 
present on one of those occasions. They were also frequently 
and carefully inspected by the combatant officers of the 
regiment, wlio naturally take a keen interest in a new and large 
draft of recruits. I assign a prominent position to all these, 
apparently, irrelevant details because they prove incontestably that Recruit Kurbir, the subject of the first case under 
report, passed successfully through many trying inspection^ 
between the 5th and 10th of June 1872, and consequently must 
have been in good health at the time. 
Recruit Kurbir, 5th Goorkha Regiment, came to hospital on 
the morning of 16th June 1872, stating that lie had- been 
feverish and out of sorts for three or four days. There was 
slight pain in the stomach which he attributed to lumbricoid 
worms. His temperature was somewhat elevated and tongue 
coated. There was no diarrhoea, nor anything either in his 
appearance or history to warrant a suspicion that he was about 
to get typhoid fever. I saw him again the following morning. 
His bowels had been moved in the meantime freely by castoroil, and he had passed a few lumbricoid worms with the 
motions. Pyrexia was still present, but to an inconsiderable 
extent. 
* I wish to explain why the notes of cases treated in regimental 
hospitals are complete enough to carry conviction as to the nature of the 
disease to any unprejudiced mind, whereas no notes worthy of record 
have been retained in connection with cases treated in the civil dispensary. 
The former occurred under my charge in regimental hospitals, and beinsl 
in a position to carry out post-mortem examinations in such cases,! was 
careful to make my notes of them as complete as circumstances permitted. 
The latter were treated n the civil dispensary, and as post-mortem examinations would be inexpedient in Frontier dispensaries, I had not the 
same motive for preserving exact notes of these cases.

April 1, 1874.] LIABILITY OP NATIVES OF INDIA TO ENTERIC EEYER, &c. 87 
Circumstances compelled me to leave Abbottabad ou the afternoon of 17th June, and when I returned at 5 p.m., on the 22nd 
the hospital assistant was so anxious about Kurbir that he 
summoned me at once to see him. I had then no difficulty in 
diagnosing enteric fever, and at once removed the man and his 
sick attendant to a separate ward.- 
The following notes, relative to the subsequent progress 
of this case, are abstracted from those recorded at the time in 
the hospital case book. It must be borne in mind that the 
hospital assistant is responsible for particulars of the case 
between the 17th and 22ud June. I merely copied into the 
book what he told me of its progress during my own absence :? 
Notes abstracted from Case Book. 
Kurbir Recruit, aged 21. 
(Enterio Fever). 
June 23rd, morning.?" On the 16th instant this boy was 
" admitted for intermittent fever complicated with lumbricoid 
"worms. The latter were expelled with the usual remedies, 
" and he was quite free from fever on 17th and 18tli.* At noon 
" 
on 19th pyrexia again appeared, and has not since left him. 
" He had looseness of bowels on the 19th and 20th, which was 
"checked by chalk mixture and astringents." 
Present state.?Lies in a stupid listless state ; skin dry and 
hot; pulse rapid ; tongue parched and leathery ; abdomen 
slightly distended and painful on pressure in both iliac regions. 
No spots can be observed on skin. Bowels have not been 
moved for twelve hours. 
" June 13rd, 1872, 'Evening visit.?No cough or chest complication. Fever increased all day, and at 6 5. M. patient was 
much relieved by profuse perspiration, which apparently 
reduced his temperature.f He is very listless and takes but

small quantities of nourishment or medicine. Tongue continues dry and hard ; pulse very rapid ; general prostration very 
marked. No diarrhoea during the day. 
"24th, Morning visit.?Passed a moderately fair night, 
sleeping at intervals, also partook of fluid nourishment freely. 
Oil the whole, patient seems rather brighter this morning. 
Skin continues hot, pulse rapid, and tongue hard and dry. 
Sordes are forming on lips and teeth. Patient winces 
and shrinks when the iliac regions are pressed, and distinct 
gurgling can always be elicited in left iliac fossa. He passed 
fluid faeces unconsciously in bed during the night. 
"24th, Evening visit.?Excessively weak and prostrate; 
pulse feeble and fluttering ; no change in tongue ; passed liquid 
fasces in bed once or twice since morning. 
"25</?, Morning visit.?Had a quiet night, but was occasionally delirious ; seems, if anything, weaker and more utterly 
prostrate ; tongue like leather ; thick sordes on teeth and gums ; 
pulse rapid and fluttering. No further diarrhoea. He coughs 
loosely now and again. 
"25th, Evening visit.?Little or no change in general 
condition of patient. His temperature seemed to increase until 
5 v. M., when he was relieved by free perspiration. His breathing 
is becoming more rapid and shallow. He refuses medicine, and 
with difficulty tukes small quantities of milk, &c. 
" 26th, Morning visit.?Passed the night in the same 
lethargic state as usual with occasional muttering delirium. 
Breathing is even more rapid than it was yesterday ; and lungs, 
more particularly the right one, are evidently congested ; pulse 
very weak and fluttering ; tongue leathery ; gums und teeth 
clogged with dense sordes. 
" Abdomen distended and painful in iliac regions ; gurgling 
is also distinct; no spots or eruption on body ; passed liquid 
motions unconsciously once or twice during the night. The 
greatest persuasion is now necessary to induce patient to swallownourishment.

" 26iA, Evening visit?Has been comatose since morning, with 
heavy oppressed breathing, and rattling in throat <md chest 
for the last two hours ; groans constantly; pulse almost imperceptible. Patient is evidently sinking rapidly. 
" He died between 8 and 9 p.m. the same evening." 
A post-mortem examination was held at 8 a.m. the following 
morning, 27th June 1872, with the following results :? 
" Body well nourished and fairly covered with fat. Rigor 
mortis slightly marked. No examination of head. Botli lungs 
much congested. Liver healthy, but stained slate colour on its 
under surface from contact with colon. The intestines were 
removed en masse to facilitate careful investigation. The mucous 
membrane of alimentary canal from stomach to within 3? feet 
of ileo-colic valve was healthy, abnormal appearances being 
limited exclusively to last 3? feet of ileum. In the upper 
portion of tliis diseased area, Beyer's patches showed infiltration, congestion, and here and there slight traces of commencing ulceration. In the middle third similar pathological 
conditions were better developed. In lower third, more especially just above the valve, infiltration was extensive, and 
ulceration further advanced, sloughs being partially detached 
in several places. Ileum contained shreds of yellow fseces tinged 
and mixed with mucus. The coecum, ascending and transverse 
colon were slate colour aud distended with dark liquid faeces. 
They were not congested, nor did they present enlarged or 
ulcerated glands." 
Remarks.?The only features in this case deserving special 
notice were:?1st, the mitigated character of the diarrhoea; 
2ndly, total absence of eruption or spots; and 3rdly, profuse 
diaphoresis with apparent decline of temperature at suuset. A 
thermometer would have proved whether the fall in temperature was imaginary or real. 
A brief summary of Case No. I appeared in the Sanitary 
Report for 1872, q. v.

Case No. II ran a course so similar in all essential points to 
No. I that I shall spare your readers details of its daily history. 
There was no doubt of this case from the beginning. 
Diarrhoea was marked although easily controlled. Pain with 
gurgling on pressure in right iliac fossa was always present. 
Diaphoresis was not observed to a marked extent at any time, 
and pyrexia steadily increased towards the evening. There 
was no eruption. 
The main features of the case may be briefly summed up as 
follows: 
No. 1410.?Dumbir Singh, Band boy, 5th Goorkha Regiment/two years' service, reputed age 20, but did not look 
more than 17 or 18. 
A previously healthy, well-nourished lad. Had been feverish 
and generally out of sorts for two or three days, but continued 
to perform his ordinary work up to the day preceding his admission on the 4th of March 1873. When first seen, on 
morning of 4th March 1873, he wa3 feverish, had slight diarrhoea aud pain, &c., in right iliac region. The disease ran a 
rapid, unfavorable course, proving fatal on 17th March, 13 days 
after his admission. Dr. Gh P. Mackenzie saw this case more 
than once, and very kindly assisted me at the post-mortem 
examination on the morning of the 18th March. 
The body, that of a youth, was somewhat emaciated, but 
showed a fair quantity of fat. Our examination wa^ chiefly 
confined to the intestinal tract which was very carefully inspected. As in the preceding case, the alimentary canal, up to 
within three feet of the termination of'the ileum, w as perfectly 
* The hospital assistant was clearly wrong in asserting that the 
man was free from fever on 17th and 18th. A clinical thermometer would 
have shown the continued nature of the pyrexia, but unfortunately native 
hospitals are not as yet supplied with these uselui instruments. 
t The absence of accurate thermoinetrical observations in this case is

xuuch to be regretted. 
88 ? THE INDIAN MEDICAL GAZETTE. [April 1, 1874. 
healthy. But, from this point to its junction with head of 
colon, the inner coat of the ileum presented all the most characteristic indications of typhoid, and richly deserved preservation 
as a typical example of the local pathological deposits and 
ulceration caused by that disease. The ccecum and colon were 
quite healthy. Dr. Mackenzie and I were so much struck with 
the appearance of the diseased end of the ileum that I preserved 
it in a wide-mouthed bottle with bazar spirits, in tlie hope of 
attracting the attention of those whose experience was so extensive as to induce them to deny positively the existence of enteric 
fever in natives, I mentioned, when officially reporting this case, 
that the intestine had been preserved ; but no notice was taken 
of my observation, nor were any enquiries made on the subject. 
Case No. Ill shewed features concerning the significance 
of which opinions may possibly vary ; I am therefore compelled 
to give it in extenso, as originally recorded, together with my 
own interpretation of the phenomena it presented. 
No. 1103.?Sepoy Khatak Bahadoor, aged 31, service nine 
years, 
" enteric fever." 
"December 12th, 1873.?History.?Hospital sheet only shews 
a few admissions for ague and once for the effects of corporal 
punishment up to 21st of last month (November), when patient 
came to hospital with dysenteric symptoms, which were readily 
subdued under ordinary treatment. Having been free from 
fever and looseness of bowels for some days he was discharged to 
duty on the 29th November. According to his own account, 
he continued well until the 4th December when fever set in, compelling him to come to hospital the following morning, 5tli of 
December. His illness was regarded as an ordinary attack 
of ague tending towards remittent fever (a total absence of 
diarrhoea or tendency to looseness of bowels gave some ground

for this belief) until this morning (12th December) when 
struck by his great prostration I examined him carefully and 
detected great pain in right iliac region. There was neither 
eruption nor diarrhoea. His disease was then changed to 
in the enteric fever. 
I was absent on leave until the 30th November, and wrote 
the accompanying particulars of the man's illness between 21st 
and 29th November from the statement of the hospital assistant. Our Goorkhas are impressed with a belief that passing 
a muster day in hospital will tell against them in some mysterious 
way, and consequently endeavour to get discharged before the 
end of the month. In pursuance of this object this Sepoy, no 
doubt, represented himself a3 quite well on 29th, and was 
accordingly discharged. At that time a thermometer would 
probably have shewn an elevation of temperature which would 
have drawn attention to his state. 
" The temperature on the morning of the 12th was 101? and 
in the evening 102?. 
"13th.?Morning temperature 101-3?: evening temperature. 
101?. Lower portion of abdomen painful; bowels not 
moved. 
" 14th.?Morning temperature 100?: evening temperature 
101?. Bowels moved twice loosely; motions tinged with blood 
and mucus. 
? 15th.?Morning temperature 98? : evening temperature 101? 
Bowels moved once loosely. 
" 16th.? Patient still prostrate, but sleeps fuirly and takes 
a moderate amount of fluid nourishment. Morning temperature 991?: evening temperature 101'3o. 
" 17th.?Slept badly, bowels being moyed three times copiously, motions fluid and tinged freely with blood and mucus. 
Pain in right iliac region and gurgling very distinct ; no 
spots. Pulse 120: temperature 101?. Tongue dry and red 
at tip and edges. Is languid and does not like being disturbed 
A few sordes are forming on lips and teeth. 
" December Vjth, 6 p.m.?General condition unchanged,

patient very weak ; tongue drier than it. was this morning; no 
spots. Abdomen free from pain, with exception of right iliac 
region, which is excessively tender on pressure. No motion 
since morning. Partakes freely of milk and arrowroot. Pulse 
126. Temperature 10280. 
" 18i&, Morning.?Passed an indifferent night, but looks 
brighter in aspect. Bowels moved scantily three times, 
motions similar to previous ones. Tongue in same dry parched condition. Pain still very great on pressure in right iliac 
region. Pulse 112. Temperature 100 8?. 
"6 p.m.?Had a fair day, no motions. Temperature 102?. 
" 19thy Morning.?Passed a fair night, had one moderately 
consistent motion at 9 p.m. Aspect and tongue improving ; 
the latter shows some signs of moisture at tip and edges. Has 
some desire for food. Pain in iliac region less. Pulse 10G. 
Temperature 98 8?. 
" 6 p. m.?Progress satisfactory ; no motions ; inclination for 
food increasing. Tongue moister. Pulse 116. Temperature 
101-4?. 
" 20th, Morning.?Slept well, bowels not moved. Aspect 
placid. Tongue is however again dry and leathery and pain 
more marked in iliac region. Seems anxious for food. Pulse 
100. Temperature 99'4?. 
" 6 p.m.?No motions. Temperature 102'6?. 
,l 
21st, Morning.?Slept fairly, bowels moved twice, motions 
large, semi-consistent and apparently quite free from blood or 
mucus. Pain still distinct in iliac region. On the whole 
patient is better. Tongue slightly moist. Patient's spirits 
are good, and he is anxious for food. Pulse intermittent, 100. 
Temperature 98'4?. 
" 6 p.m.?Temperature 102-8?. No motions. 
" 22nd, Morning.?Unchanged, takes nourishment, and gets 
broken periods of sleep. Tongue dry, pain acute on pressure 
in iliac region. Pulse 100. Temperature 99?.

" 6 p.m.'? Bowels still confined. Temperature 102-8?. 
" 23rd, Morning.?Slept fairly, but fever and restlessness have 
increased. Tongue very dry. Is unable to bear any pressure 
in right iliac region. Pulse 120. Temperature 101?. Bowels 
have acted freely, motion healthy. 
"6 p.m.?Pyrexia and general distress augmented. Temperature 104?. 
" 24th, Morning.?Passed a restless night, being much distressed by cough and fever. Breathing rapid and shallow. Tongue 
dry and glazed. Pulse feeble 140. Temperature 102'4?.

"28th, Morning. ?Much worse in every respect. Prostration extreme. Respiration rapid and shallow, 46. Pulse too 
rapid to be counted, weak and fluttering. Temperature 102'2?. 
Increased distress probably due to implication of base of left 
lung ; but this cannot be ascertained by examination, patient 
being too weak to be moved. 
" Died at 4 p.m. 
" Post-mortem examination was held at 8 a.in. on 29th December, sixteen hours after death. 
"Body emaciated. Nothing noteworthy observed externally. " Thorax.?Lower half of right lung deeply congested, and 
posterior aspect of left lung slightly so. Both sides of heart 
full of decolorised clots projecting into vessels. 
" Abdomen.?Lower portions of intestines and peritoneum 
between iliac regions slate coloured, injected and thickly covered with tenacious lymph which formed numerous adhesions. On 
attempting to separate folds of ileum, about 2 ounces of white 
purulent-looking matter escaped. When carefully detached nnd 
opened, the mucous membrane of the alimentary canal presented 
appearances as follows :?Colon healthy throughout and full 
of consistent feces. Ileum, immediately above valve, was 
much infiltrated, and in the thickened tissue there were several depressions and excavations, the sites of detached sloughs. 
Six or seven inches above valve, one mass of Peyer's patches 
shewed the characteristic typhoid deposit, and in other places 
there were a few doubtful looking depressed spots, circular and 
oblong in shape, the probable results of previous ulceration. 
All other portions of intestinal tract were healthy. I should 
have noticed before that the last foot of ileum was so firmly 
adherent to subjacent structures that I experienced great difficulty in detaching it. I could not ascertain satisfactorily the 
point of perforation, but from the depth of the ulcers there can 
be no doubt that it must have taken place in more than one 
spot just above the valve. There were two or three collections,

a couple of ounces each, of white purulent looking fluid between the fold of mesentery and ileum in close contact with 
outer coat of latter, but having no apparent communication 
with interior of the gut. These accumulations, although within 
three feet of the valve, were well above the ulcerations already 
noticed, and were not immediately connected with any lesion 
of mucous membrane of ileum. The kidneys and spleen were 
healthy ; liver also appeared healthy, but through an oversight 
was not carefully examined." 
Remarks.?On carefully reviewing all the circumstances 
attending this case together with the light thrown upon them 
by the post-mortem examination, I have come to the conclusion 
that the patient must have been suffering from mild typhoid 
fever when in hospital between the 21st and 29th November. 
He voluntarily went to the lines and no doubt resumed his 
ordinary diet while the local mischief was still active. Irritation and extension of ulceration resulted, leading to perforation 
with limited discharge of intestinal contents into peritoneum. 
Adhesive inflammation then glued the rents in ileum to subjacent structures, effectually preventing further discharge of its 
contents. The general condition of peritoneal cavity shewed 
clearly that perforation must have occurred in an early stage 
of the treatment. 
Variations and irregularities in the thermometric readings 
nro amply accounted for by the secondary lesions or accidents 
of typhoid already described. 
Case No. IV. 
The subject of the fourth case was Phandi, a Punjabi Kahar, 
aged 20 years. This man had been in Abbottabad some six 
weeks, waiting for employment, and was examined and entertained as a dooli-bearer in the 4th Punjab Infantry by Dr. J. W. 
Johnston of that Regimeut on the 22nd of January 1874. 
Phandi was admitted to hospital on 30tli January 1874, having 
been previously feverish and out of sorts for two or three 
clays in the lines. Pyrexia was then present, but an enlarged 
spleen and the generally ansemic aspect of patient induced

me to regard the case as one of ordinary remittent fever.. 
This diagnosis was confirmed by a total absences of diarrhoea, 
spots or pain in iliac regions. I looked carefully for three 
indications and warned the hospital assistant to watch for 
them in case the disease should prove to be enteri^ Unfortunately, my clinical thermometers were either broken or useless, 
so that I was unable to avail myself of this most essential aid to 
diagnosis. In this case continued absence of either diarrhoea, 
pain in abdomen, or eruption, together with the occasional occurrence of profuse diaphoresis, followed by apparent remissions 
of fever, strengthened my original opinion regarding the nature 
of the disease. The patient progressed moderately well, until 
between 8 and 9 p.m., on 8th February, when he complained 
of sudden and acute pain in abdomen. Thinking this due 
to constipation, the hospital assistant administered a dose 
of castor-oil which acted two or three times. Hot local applications to abdomen were kept up all night. When visiting 
hospital on morning of 9th February, I found the patient 
very prostrate witli a pinched distressed aspect. Surface rather 
cold, and pulse weak, rapid and thin. Both iliac, umbilical and 
hypogastric regions wero so exquisitely tender as to resent the 
slightest pressure. Epigastric and hypochondriac regions were 
distended by tympanites, and somewhat painful on pressure. 
I at once diagnosed peritonitis from perforation. 
The patient gradually got weaker, and died at 10 p m. on 
11th February. A post-mortem examination was held, in 
presence of three hospital assistants at 9 a.m. on the 12th 
February 1874. Nothing noteworthy observed externally. At 
the desire of deceased's friends only a limited examination was 
made. On opening abdomen indications of general and severe 
peritonitis were immediately observed, the viscera and peritoneum being covered with and glued together by a copious 
deposit of recent lymph. The pelvis and lower portion of 
abdomen contained a considerable quantity of feculent matter

which had escaped from the intestinal tract. 
The intestines were removed en masse, and most carefully inspected. This examination gave the following results:?Upper 
portion of jejunum healthy, lower half showed a few widely 
scattered spot of congestion, each from j to f of an inch in 
diameter. These isolated spots were too distinct to escape observation, but they were quite free from ulceration or other abrasions 
of surface. About three feet above ileo-colic valve the ileum 
presented an infiltrated mass of Peyer's glands, in the centre of 
which was a sloughing ulcer communicating with peritoneum 
by a rent about a quarter of an inch in length. Six inches lower 
down there was similar inGltration witli a smaller perforating 
ulcer in its centre. The last foot of ileum showed the 
characteristic typhoid deposit and ulceration of Peyer's patches 
in four or five distinct localities. The infiltration was most 
marked just above the valve, where I counted eight shallow 
excavations due to detached sloughs from ulcers. The colon 
contained a considerable quantity of natural faeces, and its 
mucous membrane was perfectly healthy throughout its entire 
length. . 
Remarks.?I would draw attention to the entire absence of 
rose-coloured spots or eruptions in the preceding four cases. 
These are symptoms of important diagnostic value. Yet, 
though carefully searched for by me on each occasion, I failed 
to detect them. In fact, I should have been disposed to conclude either that such eruptions were not characteristic of the 
typhoid met with in India, or that, in spite of my care, I had 
foiled to detect them had I not seen them, plainly, and urmistakeably marked in cases Nos. 5 and 9 of the following civil

Notes of a case of Acute tulerculosis, apparently originating in 
deposit and ulceration in the intestinal glands. 
No. 1305.?Sepoy Gumnn Sing, G-oorung, aged 25 years, 
service 4 years, a robust man who had enjoyed good health 
until the first week of March 1873, when he was admitted to 
hospital with what appeared to be, an ordinary attack of 
intermittent fever. His liver projected an inch below level 
of ribs, and was now and again tender on pressure. There 
was a tendency to looseness of bowels which was easily kept 
in check. "When fever was present the morning temperature 
exceeded that of the afternoon by from one to two degrees. 
The fever however was not constant, and occasionally disappeared for several days in succession. From the time of 
admission until the middle of June, it was impossible to assign 
these recurring attacks of low fever and patient's cachectic 
appearance to any specific cause. The lungs were healthy, 
diarrhoea so slight as scarcely to attract attention, and nothing 
abnormal could be detected in abdomen with the exception 
of enlargement of liver. 
On the 20th of June, when examining patient's abdomen, h6 
drew my attention to a small nodulated tumour situated just 
beneath the navel. It was movable, and could not be felt at all 
when the intestines were distended. In the second week of 
July, a EiOnth after the abdominal tumour became manifest, 
he first began to cough, and from that time the downward progress of the case was extremely rapid. For all practical purposes sufficient details of its subsequent history can be gathered 
from the following notes taken at intervals from the regimental case book:? 
July 20th, 1873.?Patient rather emaciated and ancemic; 
cough frequent; expectoration thick but scanty ; pulse 108 ; 
temperature 102? 5 tongue clean and red at edges; infra clavicular 
region of left thorax dull on percussion ; bronchial respiration 
accompanied with mucus rales audible under dull area. The

breathing in apex of right lung is also slightly bronchial in 
character. A tumour about the size of a large lime and kidney-shaped can be felt and moved slightly from side to side 
below navel. 
August 5th.?Dulness very marked below left clavicle where 
lung tissue appears to be rapidly breaking up. Respiration in 
right apex weak and accompanied with mucus rales. Morning temperature generally from 1 to 1? degree above that of 
evening. 
7th.?Yesterday diarrhoea recurred, bowels being moved 
loosely five or six times. The temperature which for several 
preceding days had never been under 101o or 102? suddenly 
fell to 100?> at which it now stands. Pulse small and rapid ; 
skin soft and moist. Although much weaker, patient seems 
relieved by the diarrhoea. 
14th.?Much in same state ; temperature averaging 1002o ; 
bowels moved about four times in 24 hours; motions thin 
and serous ; cough easier during the day, but at night extremely 
troublesome, interfering greatly with sleep; expectoration 
abundant, thick, and with a heavy offensive odour. Has 
perspired freely for last few nights. 
2,\st.?Excessively emaciated and exhausted ; appears to be 
sinking; unable to speak, and only occasionally recognizes 
his friends; cough and diarrhoea persist; liver, probably 
in consequence of general emaciation, appears more prominent 
than before; pulse weak and rapid. Died at 12 noon the 
same day. Post-mortem examination held at 5 p.m. 
Body much wasted. Extensive cavities in apices of both 
lungs, the rest of these organs being densely studded with 
miliary tubercles; liver' much enlarged ; mesenteric glands 
enormously distended with tubercular deposit, which on 
section presented a clieese-like appearance. In small 
intestines at intervals varying from three or four to 
several inches were found small circular ulcers, having a punched out aspect. These ulcers were generally so deep as to

have involved all but the peritoneal coat of intestine. They 
were not more numerous in the typhoid area than in other 
place3, and clearly represented the remains of solitary glands. 
The agminated glands were not perceptibly affected. In this 
case tubercular deposit evidently first occurred in the solitary 
intestinal glands. The mesenteric glands were next affected, 
and finally the system at large became involved in the condition known as acute tuberculosis.
